title: Keep the Practice, Recheck the Conditions
subtitle: A practical way to think about strength training during pregnancy—without assuming one routine, load or progression fits everyone.
imageAlt: A pregnant person and a training partner pause beside a bench and light dumbbells to talk through a strength session.
imageConcept: two women friends with distinct personal style together, in a specific visual scene about “Keep the Practice, Recheck the Conditions”: A relaxed, everyday training space with a pregnant person and a supportive friend or partner reviewing a simple workout together; weights are visible but not staged as a performance, and the mood is attentive rather than instructional.
body: Strength can stay in the picture

Pregnancy does not automatically mean putting strength training on hold. For people with uncomplicated pregnancies, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists encourages aerobic and strength-conditioning exercise, while emphasizing that individual medical circumstances matter and that clinical evaluation should guide exercise recommendations. That is a useful starting point—not a guarantee that every movement, position or previous training plan remains appropriate throughout pregnancy.[1]

A better question than “Can I keep doing my usual workout?” is “Does this session still fit the conditions I’m in today?” Those conditions can include clinical advice, energy, balance, comfort, equipment and how a movement feels. Adapting is not a failure of consistency. It is one way to keep a practice responsive, rather than treating the plan as more important than the person doing it.

Before deciding what to continue, ask your prenatal care team whether you have any medical or obstetric considerations that affect exercise. This is especially important if a complication has developed, your activity has been restricted, or you are considering a substantial change to a demanding training routine. ACOG advises careful evaluation when complications are present.[1]

Bring specific questions instead of asking for a blanket “all clear.” For example: “Are there movements or positions you want me to avoid?” “Should I change anything about lifting or straining?” “What symptoms mean I should stop and contact you?” If you already work with a coach, physical therapist or other exercise professional, ask what information your care team is comfortable sharing. The point is to connect relevant expertise while keeping medical decisions with your prenatal team.
Keep the targets in their lanes

Public-health guidance can be useful, but it is easy to apply a number to the wrong kind of exercise. The CDC recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week for healthy pregnant and postpartum people, and advises pregnant readers to ask a health professional whether or how to adjust activity. That is an aerobic-activity recommendation; it does not set a weekly strength-training dose, ideal number of sets or progression for lifting.[2]

ACOG says women who were regular exercisers before pregnancy and have uncomplicated, healthy pregnancies should generally be able to engage in high-intensity exercise; those who were sedentary before pregnancy should progress more gradually.[1] These principles support continuity and gradual change, but they do not supply a universal resistance program. Let the guidance inform a conversation, not substitute for one.
Use a three-part check before a session

A short check-in can help translate broad guidance into a decision you can make today. First, recall your current care-team advice: has anything changed, or is there a question you need answered before training? Second, notice your starting point: energy, steadiness, discomfort and whether you feel able to concentrate. Third, look at the session itself: does the setup feel stable, and can you perform the planned movement without forcing a position or breath?

If one answer raises a concern, scale back, choose a different movement or skip the session while you seek advice. If things feel comfortable and no restrictions apply, begin conservatively and give yourself permission to reassess after a set. This is not a screening tool and cannot diagnose a problem. It is a practical pause that helps you avoid treating last week’s capacity as a promise about today.
Adapt the movement, not your worth

Changes in comfort, balance and the effects of certain positions can influence exercise during pregnancy. ACOG discusses pregnancy-related changes that can affect activity, including balance and lying on the back after 20 weeks.[1] Rather than turning that into a rigid rule for every exercise, use it as a prompt to ask whether a position remains comfortable and appropriate for you, and follow your care team’s advice.

For example, if a floor-based press feels awkward to get into or out of, ask whether a supported seated or inclined version is a better fit. If a standing exercise feels less steady, a stable support or a different position may help—or that movement may not be right for that day. Reducing a load, range of motion or number of repetitions is also a legitimate adjustment. These are options to discuss and test carefully, not a pregnancy-specific prescription. The useful measure is not whether the session resembles your previous one; it is whether the choice suits your current circumstances.

There is growing research on resistance training in pregnancy, but the details needed to prescribe one proven routine are not consistently available. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis included 50 studies and 47,619 participants. The authors report that most exercise programs were multicomponent, and that resistance-training prescription, progression and loading were often poorly reported.[3]

That limitation matters. It means the evidence does not establish a single load, schedule or progression as safest or best for every pregnancy. It also does not mean strength exercise has no place; ACOG’s guidance supports strength-conditioning exercise in uncomplicated pregnancies.[1] The balanced reading is that strength work may remain part of an active life, while the specifics need to be individualized and the research continues to develop. Confidence here means being clear about both what guidance supports and what it cannot yet settle.
Know when the plan becomes a pause

A session is not something to push through at all costs. Stop exercising and contact your care team for guidance if you experience concerning symptoms, or if a movement brings on pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness, bleeding, fluid leakage or contractions. Ask your clinician in advance which symptoms warrant an urgent call in your particular situation; do not rely on a workout plan or online checklist to assess a possible complication.

It can help to write the care team’s instructions somewhere easy to find, especially if you train with someone else. If symptoms occur, stop, get to a safe position and follow those instructions. A training partner can help with practical support, but should not be expected to diagnose what is happening. Stopping is a sound decision when the conditions change; it does not erase the work you have already done.
Make the next session easier to choose

After training—or after deciding not to train—note what was useful: which positions felt comfortable, whether balance or setup changed your choice, and what you would like to ask your care team. Keep the note simple. It is not a scorecard, and a missed or modified session is not evidence that you lack commitment. The record is there to make the next conversation more concrete and to reduce the pressure to remember every detail on the spot.

For your next workout, choose one familiar movement and make a deliberate check before you begin: confirm that it fits the latest advice, set up a stable option, and decide what would make you stop or change course. If you are unsure, hold the question for your prenatal team rather than guessing at a rule. A strength practice that adapts can still be a practice—one built around attention, choice and care, not a demand to perform the same way every time.
